title: Functions
summary: Write functions for bike trip analysis. Convert units, work inside mutate(), summarise trips, accept column names, and build a chart with its own title.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse)
steps.explain: Every function in this lesson is built from tidyverse functions: once written, a function of your own works just like theirs.

steps.title: A first function

runs.purpose: write a function, `km_to_miles()`, that converts kilometres to miles
runs.task: Write a function called `km_to_miles` with one argument, `km`, that returns `km * 0.621371`.

steps.explain:
A function has a name, arguments, and a body: `function(km) { … }` makes one, and `<-` keeps it under a name, as for any other value. Its body uses its argument, and the last value it works out is what it returns.

The rule of thumb is to write a function once you have copied and pasted the same code three times: the conversion factor then lives in one place, and the name says what the code is for. Arithmetic works on vectors, so `km_to_miles()` converts all three distances at once.

steps.title: Vector functions in mutate()

runs.purpose: write `speed_kmh()`, which works out speed in km/h from a distance and a time in minutes
runs.task: Write `speed_kmh`, a function of `km` and `minutes` that returns `km / minutes * 60`.

alternatives: trips |> transmute(distance_km, duration_min, speed = speed_kmh(km = distance_km, minutes = duration_min))
runs.purpose: add each trip's speed with the new function
runs.task: Add `speed`, made with `speed_kmh(distance_km, duration_min)`, keeping only the columns used.

steps.explain:
A vector function takes vectors and returns one of the same length, so it fits in `mutate()`, where each argument is a whole column: the first trip's speed is {first_speed} km/h. Inside the function, `km` and `minutes` are just names for whatever was passed in, here `distance_km` and `duration_min`.

Arguments match by position, as here, or by name, `speed_kmh(km = …, minutes = …)`.

steps.title: Summary functions

alternatives: share_of = function(x, value) mean(x == value, na.rm = TRUE)
runs.purpose: write `share_of()`, which gives the share of a vector equal to a value
runs.task: Write `share_of`, a function of `x` and `value` that returns `mean(x == value, na.rm = TRUE)`.

runs.purpose: find the share of e-bike trips for each rider type
runs.task: For each `member_type`, find the share of trips with `bike_type` "electric", using `share_of()` in `summarize()`.

steps.explain:
A summary function turns a vector into a single value, so it fits in `summarize()`. `share_of()` packs lesson 12's trick, the mean of a condition, behind a name that says what it means.

A function that needs a default for a rarely changed argument gets one in its definition: `function(x, value, na.rm = TRUE)` would let a caller turn off the dropping of missing values.

steps.title: Data frame functions: {{ }}

alternatives: summarize_trips = function(df, group) df |> summarize(trips = n(), median_minutes = median(duration_min), .by = {{ group }})
runs.purpose: write `summarize_trips()`, which counts trips and finds their median length for any grouping column
runs.task: Write `summarize_trips`, a function of `df` and `group`, that summarises `df` with `trips = n()` and `median_minutes = median(duration_min)`, grouped `.by = {{ group }}`.

runs.purpose: summarise the trips by rider type with it
and by rider type and bike type together
runs.task: Call it again, grouping by `c(member_type, bike_type)`.

steps.explain:
dplyr lets you write column names bare, `.by = member_type`, because it looks them up in the data. Inside a function, though, `group` is the function's argument, and `.by = group` would look for a column called group. Embracing it, `{{ group }}`, tells dplyr to use whatever the caller wrote in its place, here `member_type`, or `c(member_type, bike_type)`.

Embrace every argument that names columns.

steps.title: Plot functions

alternatives: duration_histogram = function(df, binwidth = 2) ggplot(df, aes(duration_min)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = binwidth) + labs(title = str_glue('{nrow(df)} trips'))
runs.purpose: write `duration_histogram()`, which draws a histogram of trip lengths titled with how many trips it shows
runs.task: Write `duration_histogram(df, binwidth = 2)`. It draws a histogram of `duration_min` with that bin width, titled with `str_glue("{nrow(df)} trips")`.

runs.purpose: draw the histogram for casual riders' trips of under two hours
runs.task: Keep casual riders' trips longer than 0 and shorter than 120 minutes, then pipe them into `duration_histogram()`.

steps.explain:
A function can return a chart as easily as a number. `binwidth = 2` gives the argument a default, so a caller can leave it out. The title is worked out from the data, so it always says how many trips are drawn: {n_casual}.

Name functions with verbs or descriptions of what they return, and arguments with nouns, data first, so that functions work with the pipe.
